# Dates and Times {#sec-lubridate}



Dates are everywhere in audit. A bill has a date of receipt and a date of payment. A contract has a period of validity. A rate has a date from which it is in force. An employee has a date of birth, a date of joining and a date of retirement. Many audit questions are really questions about dates. Was the bill paid within the time allowed? Was a payment made on a Sunday or a gazetted holiday? Was the rate applied the one in force on the date of the bill? How long have these advances been pending?

Computerised systems also record the *time* of each action. A treasury's e-payment system notes when each payment was approved. A payment approved at two in the morning is not necessarily wrong. But it deserves a question.

Dates are also easy to get wrong. One office writes 05/04/2024 for the 5th of April, and a spreadsheet reads it as the 4th of May. A time stamp stored in UTC looks five and a half hours early when read as Indian time. A month added to the 31st of January lands on a date that does not exist. In this chapter we learn to handle dates and times correctly. We start with the base R classes for dates and times. We then learn the package `lubridate`, which makes the work much easier. Finally, we apply both to a register of bills and a log of e-payment approvals, and find payments on holidays, long-pending bills and approvals made late at night.

**Prerequisites**


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
```
:::


The package `lubridate` is part of the core tidyverse, so `library(tidyverse)` loads it too.

## Our data, a register of bills {#sec-lubri-data}

Through the chapter, we use the register of bills received by an office over two financial years, 2023-24 and 2024-25. Each bill has the date it was received, the date it was paid and the amount. Bills not yet paid on 31 March 2025 have no payment date. A few irregular payments are planted in the data. We will find them in @sec-lubri-audit. The code below creates the register. It uses several functions which we learn in this chapter, so new readers may come back to it later.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Code to create the bill register"}
set.seed(1947)
n <- 400
bill_register <- tibble(
  bill_no  = sprintf("BL-%04d", 1:n),
  received = as.Date("2023-04-01") + sample(0:700, n, TRUE),
  amount   = round(rlnorm(n, log(60000), 0.9))
) |>
  mutate(paid = received + round(rexp(n, 1 / 20)))

# Genuine payments are made on working days. Move Sundays and holidays forward.
holidays <- as.Date(c("2024-01-26", "2024-08-15", "2024-10-02",
                      "2025-01-26", "2025-08-15", "2025-10-02"))
for (k in 1:2) {
  off <- wday(bill_register$paid, week_start = 1) == 7 | bill_register$paid %in% holidays
  bill_register$paid[off] <- bill_register$paid[off] + 1
}

# Some bills are still unpaid on 31 March 2025
unpaid <- sample(1:n, 45)
bill_register$paid[unpaid] <- NA
# Payments dated after 31 March 2025 have not happened yet
bill_register$paid[which(bill_register$paid > as.Date("2025-03-31"))] <- NA
# Planted. A few payments made on Sundays and on Independence Day
bill_register$paid[c(12, 57, 133, 260)] <- as.Date(c("2024-06-09", "2024-08-15",
                                                      "2024-11-17", "2025-01-26"))
```
:::

## Base R classes to deal with date and time variables

R has four core classes for dates and times.

-   `Date` for dates. (Note the capital `D`.)
-   `POSIXct` for date-times.
-   `POSIXlt` for date-times, stored differently. The difference is explained in @sec-timm.
-   `difftime` for time spans.

### Dates

The base R function `as.Date()` turns text into a `Date`. It takes a character vector and, optionally, the format in which the date is written. The default format is year, month and day, separated by hyphens. Registers in Indian offices usually write the day first, so we give the format ourselves.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
as.Date("2024-12-12")                        # default format
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-12-12"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
as.Date("12-12-2024", format = "%d-%m-%Y")   # day first, as in most registers
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-12-12"
```


:::
:::


We can check the `class` of the object created.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
bill_date <- as.Date("20-12-2024", format = "%d-%m-%Y")
class(bill_date)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Date"
```


:::
:::


The format uses special codes, like `%d` for the day and `%Y` for a four-digit year. Run `?strptime` in your console to see them all. A ready reference for the most used codes is in @tbl-lubri001 in @sec-strpp.

Behind the scenes, a date is stored as a number, the count of days since an *origin*, 1 January 1970.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
class(bill_date)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Date"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
typeof(bill_date)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "double"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
unclass(bill_date)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 20077
```


:::
:::


So, in R 4.3.0 and later, `as.Date()` also accepts a number, and counts that many days from the origin.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
as.Date(1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "1970-01-02"
```


:::
:::


The date one day after the default origin, 1970-01-01, is returned. The argument `origin` changes the starting point. This is very useful in audit. Excel also stores dates as numbers, but counts from 30 December 1899. When an Excel file is read carelessly, the dates arrive as numbers like 45383. The right origin turns them back into dates.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# A date that arrived from Excel as a number
as.Date(45383, origin = "1899-12-30")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-04-01"
```


:::
:::


### Times {#sec-timm}

To create date-time objects, we use `as.POSIXct()` or `as.POSIXlt()`. Here is the time stamp of a payment approval, written in two ways.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
as.POSIXct("2024/11/17 12:20:05")   # default format
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-11-17 12:20:05 IST"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
as.POSIXct("17-11-2024 15:30:00", format = "%d-%m-%Y %H:%M:%S")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-11-17 15:30:00 IST"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
as.POSIXlt("17-11-2024 15:30:00", format = "%d-%m-%Y %H:%M:%S")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-11-17 15:30:00 IST"
```


:::
:::


The two classes store the same moment differently. `POSIXct` stores the number of *seconds* since the origin. `POSIXlt` stores a list of parts, the *day*, *month*, *year*, *hour*, *minute*, *second* and a few more. The code below shows both.

::: callout-note
`ct` in `POSIXct` stands for calendar time, and `lt` in `POSIXlt` stands for local time. This explains the difference in how they are stored.
:::


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
time_ct <- as.POSIXct("17-11-2024 15:30:00", format = "%d-%m-%Y %H:%M:%S")
class(time_ct)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "POSIXct" "POSIXt" 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
unclass(time_ct)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1731837600
attr(,"tzone")
[1] ""
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
## POSIXlt
# Convert the above object into POSIXlt
time_lt <- as.POSIXlt(time_ct)
# Let us print it
time_lt
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-11-17 15:30:00 IST"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
class(time_lt)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "POSIXlt" "POSIXt" 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
unclass(time_lt)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

$min

attr(,"tzone")

```


:::
:::


Like `as.Date()`, `as.POSIXct()` also accepts a number, and counts that many seconds from the origin.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
as.POSIXct(60)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "1970-01-01 05:31:00 IST"
```


:::
:::


### Times (without dates)

Base R has no class for a time of day without a date. The package `hms`, part of the tidyverse, fills this gap. It is handy for things like the office opening time.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
hms::as_hms("09:30:00")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
09:30:00
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
hms::as_hms(10)          # ten seconds
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
00:00:10
```


:::
:::


### Timespan {#sec-diffftime}

Subtracting one date from another gives an object of the special class `difftime`. It holds the difference, with its unit. Let us take a bill received on 2 August 2024 and paid on 20 September 2024.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
(days_taken <- as.Date("2024-09-20") - as.Date("2024-08-02"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Time difference of 49 days
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
class(days_taken)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "difftime"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
unclass(days_taken)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 49
attr(,"units")
[1] "days"
```


:::
:::


The bill took 49 days to pay. If it was from a micro or small enterprise, that is beyond the 45 days allowed by law.

The function `difftime()` gives the difference in a unit of our choice. The argument `units` takes one of `"auto"`, `"secs"`, `"mins"`, `"hours"`, `"days"` or `"weeks"`.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
difftime(as.Date("2024-09-20"), as.Date("2024-08-02"), units = "weeks")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Time difference of 7 weeks
```


:::
:::


We can also create a difftime object directly, for example a time limit of 15 days.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
time_limit <- as.difftime(15, units = "days")
time_limit
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Time difference of 15 days
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
class(time_limit)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "difftime"
```


:::
:::


### Time zones

The function `Sys.timezone()` gives the time zone of your computer. `OlsonNames()` lists all the time zones R knows. Indian Standard Time is `"Asia/Kolkata"`.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
Sys.timezone()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Asia/Calcutta"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
grep("Kolkata|London", OlsonNames(), value = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Asia/Kolkata"  "Europe/London"
```


:::
:::


The `tz` argument of `as.POSIXct()` and `as.POSIXlt()` gives the time zone when turning numbers or text into date-times. The same number of seconds is a different clock time in each zone.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
as.POSIXct(1, tz = "GMT")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "1970-01-01 00:00:01 GMT"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
as.POSIXct(1, tz = "Asia/Kolkata")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "1970-01-01 05:30:01 IST"
```


:::
:::


### Coercion

We have already met the functions which convert objects from one class to another.

- `as.Date()`
- `as.POSIXct()`
- `as.POSIXlt()`
- `as.difftime()`

### Extracting parts from dates/times

Base R has some useful functions to extract parts of a date.

- `weekdays(x, abbreviate = FALSE)` gives the name of the day of the week, as text.
- `months(x, abbreviate = FALSE)` gives the name of the month, as text.
- `quarters(x)` gives the calendar quarter, as text.
- `julian(x)` gives the number of days since the origin, as a number.

Let us take the dates of one week in August 2024.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
dates_vec <- seq(as.Date("2024-08-12"), by = "day", length.out = 7)
weekdays(dates_vec)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Monday"    "Tuesday"   "Wednesday" "Thursday"  "Friday"    "Saturday" 
[7] "Sunday"   
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
months(dates_vec)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "August" "August" "August" "August" "August" "August" "August"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
quarters(dates_vec)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Q3" "Q3" "Q3" "Q3" "Q3" "Q3" "Q3"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
julian(dates_vec)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 19947 19948 19949 19950 19951 19952 19953
attr(,"origin")
[1] "1970-01-01"
```


:::
:::


The 15th of August, Independence Day, was a Thursday. `quarters()` gives calendar quarters, so August is in `Q3`. For the Indian financial year, which begins in April, we need another way, which we see in @sec-lubri-audit.

### Other useful related functions

The function `seq()` on dates, also written `seq.Date()`, makes a sequence of dates. Its syntax is `seq.Date(from, to, by, length.out = NULL, along.with = NULL, ...)`. The arguments are these.

- `from` and `to` are the start and end dates.
- `by` is the step. It can be one of the following.
    + A number, taken as days.
    + An object of class `difftime`.
    + A text value, one of "day", "week", "month", "quarter" or "year". It can have a whole number and a space before it, like "2 weeks", or an "s" after it.
- `length.out` is the desired length of the sequence. It is optional.
- `along.with` takes the length from the length of this argument.

For example, the first day of each month of the financial year 2024-25 is given below.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
seq(as.Date("2024/4/1"), by = "month", length.out = 12)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 [1] "2024-04-01" "2024-05-01" "2024-06-01" "2024-07-01" "2024-08-01"
 [6] "2024-09-01" "2024-10-01" "2024-11-01" "2024-12-01" "2025-01-01"
[11] "2025-02-01" "2025-03-01"
```


:::
:::


### `strptime` character codes {#sec-strpp}

The table below lists the format codes most useful for reading and writing dates and date-times. To know more, see the output of `?strptime()` in your console.


|     Format     | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|:------------------:|----------------------------------------------------|
| `%y` (or `%Y`) | Year without (or with) century                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|      `%m`      | Month as a number (01 to 12)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `%B` (or `%b`) | Month name in full (or abbreviated) in the current locale                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|      `%d`      | Day of the month (01 to 31)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|      `%H`      | Hours as a number (00 to 23)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|      `%I`      | Hours as a number, in 12 hour format (01 to 12)                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|      `%M`      | Minute as a number (00 to 59)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|      `%S`      | Second as a whole number (00 to 61), allowing up to two leap seconds                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|     `%OS`      | Seconds with decimals                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|      `%T`      | Same as `%H:%M:%S`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|      `%p`      | AM/PM indicator in the locale                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `%A` (or `%a`) | Full (or abbreviated) name of the day of the week, in the current locale                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|      `%j`      | Day of the year as a number (001 to 366). For input, 366 is valid only in a leap year.                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|      `%u`      | Day of the week as a number (1 to 7, Monday is 1)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|      `%w`      | Day of the week as a number (0 to 6, Sunday is 0)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|      `%U`      | Week of the year as a number (00 to 53), with Sunday as the first day of the week. Typically the first Sunday of the year is day 1 of week 1. **The US convention.**                                                                                             |
|      `%V`      | Week of the year as a number (01 to 53) as defined in ISO 8601. If the week (starting on Monday) containing 1 January has four or more days in the new year, it is week 1. Otherwise, it is the last week of the previous year, and the next week is week 1. |
|      `%W`      | Week of the year as a number (00 to 53), with Monday as the first day of the week. Typically the first Monday of the year is day 1 of week 1. **The UK convention.**                                                                                                   |
|      `%z`      | Offset from UTC                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|      `%Z`      | Time zone name                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

## Creating and reading dates with `lubridate`

The package `lubridate`, now part of the core tidyverse, makes work with dates and times much easier. Creating dates and converting text or numbers into dates is simpler than in base R. It also offers classes for time spans which make calculations on periods safer.

### Date/date-time objects creation

Dates and date-times in `lubridate` are the same classes as in base R. So we can create a date (or a date-time) from a number of days (or seconds) since the origin.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(lubridate, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
# Creation using numbers
as_date(19905)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-07-01"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
as_datetime(1719838800)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-07-01 13:00:00 UTC"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Converting from one type to another
(date_today <- as_date(now()))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2026-10-05"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Check its class
class(date_today)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Date"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Or see what is inside
unclass(date_today)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 20731
```


:::
:::


### Parsing date/date-time objects from `character`

`lubridate` has a family of functions to read dates and date-times from text. Each function is named after the order in which the parts are written. Year is `y`, quarter is `q`, month is `m`, day is `d`, hour is `h`, minute is `m` and second is `s`. The separators between the parts do not matter. The functions are listed below.

- `ymd_hms`, `ymd_hm`, `ymd_h`, `ymd`
- `dmy_hms`, `dmy_hm`, `dmy_h`, `dmy`
- `mdy_hms`, `mdy_hm`, `mdy_h`, `mdy`
- `ydm_hms`, `ydm_hm`, `ydm_h`, `ydm`
- `myd`, `dym`
- `yq`, `ym`, `my`

A few examples follow, written the way dates appear in bank statements, registers and returns.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ymd("20240720")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-07-20"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
dmy("01.12.2024")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-12-01"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
dmy("15th of January, 2025")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-01-15"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
mdy_hm("August 15th, 2024 at 10:45 PM")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-08-15 22:45:00 UTC"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
my("04-2024")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-04-01"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
yq("2024: Quarter 4")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-10-01"
```


:::
:::


This flexibility is a great help with data typed by hand. The same date, written in four different ways in one register, is read correctly by one call.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
dmy(c("01/04/2024", "1-4-2024", "01.04.2024", "1st April 2024"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-04-01" "2024-04-01" "2024-04-01" "2024-04-01"
```


:::
:::


To get a date-time from a decimal year, we use `date_decimal()`.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
date_decimal(2024.162)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-02-29 07:00:28 UTC"
```


:::
:::


### Parsing dates/date-times from individual components

Some registers keep the day, month and year in separate columns. The functions `make_date()` and `make_datetime()` put them together. Their syntax is shown below.

```
make_datetime(
  year = 1970L,
  month = 1L,
  day = 1L,
  hour = 0L,
  min = 0L,
  sec = 0,
  tz = "UTC"
)

make_date(year = 1970L, month = 1L, day = 1L)
```


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
make_date(year = 1947, month = 8, day = 15)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "1947-08-15"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
tibble(bill_day = c(5, 18, 30), bill_month = c(4, 11, 2), bill_year = 2024) |>
  mutate(bill_date = make_date(bill_year, bill_month, bill_day))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  bill_day bill_month bill_year bill_date 
     <dbl>      <dbl>     <dbl> <date>    
1        5          4      2024 2024-04-05
2       18         11      2024 2024-11-18
3       30          2      2024 NA        
```


:::
:::


The third bill is dated 30 February, which does not exist, so its date is `NA`. In audit, such a row is itself a finding. It points to a data entry error, or a register filled in carelessly.

## Extracting and setting date/date-time components

### Extraction

The parts of a date or date-time are extracted with simply named functions, listed below. Note that each name is singular, like `year()`. The plural forms, like `years()`, do something else, which we see in @sec-perriod.

- `year()` for the year, and `isoyear()` for the ISO 8601 year.
- `semester()` for the half year.
- `quarter()` for the quarter.
- `month()` for the month.
- `week()` for the week of the year, and `isoweek()` for the ISO 8601 week.
- `day()` for the day of the month, `wday()` for the day of the week, and `qday()` for the day of the quarter.
- `hour()`, `minute()` and `second()` for the hour, minute and second.
- `tz()` for the time zone.

Let us take the time stamp of a payment approval.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# An approval time stamp
(a_time <- ymd_hms("2024-11-17 23:46:40", tz = "Asia/Kolkata"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-11-17 23:46:40 IST"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Day of the month
day(a_time)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 17
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Name of the day of the week, in full
wday(a_time, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] Sunday
7 Levels: Sunday < Monday < Tuesday < Wednesday < Thursday < ... < Saturday
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Seconds
second(a_time)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 40
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Name of the month, abbreviated
month(a_time, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] Nov
12 Levels: Jan < Feb < Mar < Apr < May < Jun < Jul < Aug < Sep < ... < Dec
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Week number of the year
week(a_time)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 46
```


:::
:::


The approval was made on a Sunday, at a quarter to midnight. We return to such approvals in @sec-lubri-hours.

A few functions answer yes or no questions about a date-time.

- `am(x)` and `pm(x)` tell whether `x` is before or after noon.
- `dst(x)` tells whether `x` is in daylight saving time.
- `leap_year(x)` tells whether `x` is in a leap year.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Was the approval before noon?
am(a_time)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] FALSE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Is it in a leap year?
leap_year(a_time)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Is it in daylight saving time? (India does not use it)
dst(a_time)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] FALSE
```


:::
:::


### Setting components

The same functions can also *change* a part of a date. Suppose the year of a time stamp was keyed in wrongly.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Initial value
a_time
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-11-17 23:46:40 IST"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Set the year
year(a_time) <- 2025
a_time
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-11-17 23:46:40 IST"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Set the time zone
tz(a_time) <- "UTC"
a_time
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-11-17 23:46:40 UTC"
```


:::
:::


Notice that setting the time zone kept the clock time and changed only the zone. So it now stands for a different moment. We return to this trap in the Audit tip of @sec-lubri-hours.

The function `update()` returns a date with the given parts changed, in one step.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
due_date <- dmy("31-01-2024")
due_date <- update(due_date, year = 2025)
due_date
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-01-31"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# If the new date does not exist, it rolls over into the next month
update(due_date, month = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-03-03"
```


:::
:::


There is no 31 February, so the date rolled over to 3 March. Keep this in mind when computing due dates.

## Time spans

Subtracting one date-time from another in base R gives a `difftime` object, as we saw in @sec-diffftime.

But not every unit of time has a fixed length. A year may have 365 or 366 days. Some countries use daylight saving time, so not every day there has 24 hours. To be clear about what we mean, `lubridate` has three classes of time span. They may sound alike, but they work differently.

- `period`
- `duration`
- `interval`

Let us take each in turn.

### Periods {#sec-perriod}

A *period* follows the clock and the calendar. One year is one calendar year, whatever its number of days. Periods are created with the **plural** names of the date parts, like `years()`, `months()` and `days()`.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
(one_year <- years(1))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "1y 0m 0d 0H 0M 0S"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
class(one_year)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Period"
attr(,"package")
[1] "lubridate"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# A contract of one year from 1 March 2023 ends on
contract_start <- dmy("01-03-2023")
contract_start + years(1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-03-01"
```


:::
:::


### Durations

A *duration* is an exact length of time, in seconds. Durations are created by adding `d` before the plural names, like `dyears()` and `ddays()`. One duration year is 365.25 days.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
(one_year_duration <- dyears(1))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "31557600s (~1 years)"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
class(one_year_duration)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Duration"
attr(,"package")
[1] "lubridate"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# One duration year from 1 March 2023
contract_start + dyears(1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-02-29 06:00:00 UTC"
```


:::
:::


Since 2024 is a leap year, 365.25 days from 1 March 2023 ends at 6 am on 29 February 2024, not on 1 March. For contract periods, leave and service, which follow the calendar, use periods.

### Intervals

An *interval* is a specific stretch of the time line, with a definite start and end. It is created with the function `interval()`, whose syntax is shown below.

```
interval(start = NULL, end = NULL, tzone = tz(start))
```

Let us take a rate contract valid for the financial year 2024-25.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
(contract <- interval(dmy("01-04-2024"), dmy("31-03-2025")))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2024-04-01 UTC--2025-03-31 UTC
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
class(contract)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Interval"
attr(,"package")
[1] "lubridate"
```


:::
:::


Intervals can also be created with the special operator `%--%`. Here is the period in which a work was executed.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
(work_period <- dmy("15-06-2024") %--% dmy("14-12-2024"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2024-06-15 UTC--2024-12-14 UTC
```


:::
:::


## Performing calculations on intervals/dates

`lubridate` has several functions for working with intervals.

### `%within%` operator

`a %within% b` checks whether the interval or date `a` falls within the interval `b`. It returns `TRUE` or `FALSE`.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
work_period %within% contract
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


It works on many dates at once. Supplies billed under the rate contract must fall within its validity.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
supply_dates <- dmy(c("20-03-2024", "10-10-2024", "05-04-2025"))
supply_dates %within% contract
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE
```


:::
:::


The first and the third supplies fall outside the contract period. They cannot claim the contract rate, and the auditor would ask on what terms they were bought.

### Backward intervals

Intervals in `lubridate` can run backwards, with the end before the start. This often signals an entry error, like a completion date earlier than the start date.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
(back_interval <- dmy("26-01-2025") %--% dmy("15-01-2025"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2025-01-26 UTC--2025-01-15 UTC
```


:::
:::


### Flipping intervals

The function `int_flip()` reverses the direction of an interval.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
int_flip(back_interval)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2025-01-15 UTC--2025-01-26 UTC
```


:::
:::


### Checking alignment of two intervals

The function `int_aligns()` tests whether two intervals share a start or an end. The direction of each interval is ignored. Let us take three rate contracts.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
int1 <- interval(ymd("2024-04-01"), ymd("2025-03-31"))
int2 <- interval(ymd("2024-10-01"), ymd("2025-03-31"))
int3 <- interval(ymd("2025-04-01"), ymd("2026-03-31"))

int_aligns(int1, int2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
int_aligns(int1, int3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] FALSE
```


:::
:::


### Checking overlap in two intervals

The function `int_overlaps()` tests whether two intervals overlap.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
int_overlaps(int1, int2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
int_overlaps(int1, int3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] FALSE
```


:::
:::


If `int1` and `int2` were two rate contracts for the same item, the overlap would be a question for audit. Which rate applied in the months both were valid? To compare many periods across two tables at once, overlap joins are more convenient (@sec-nonequi).

### Length of the interval

The function `int_length()` gives the length of an interval in seconds. For a backward interval, the length is negative.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
int_length(back_interval)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] -950400
```


:::
:::


### Adding months without going past the end of the month

The operators `%m+%` and `%m-%` add (or subtract) months to a date without going past the last day of the new month.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
(leap <- ymd("2024-02-29"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-02-29"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
leap %m+% years(1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-02-28"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
leap %m+% years(-1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2023-02-28"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
leap %m-% years(1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2023-02-28"
```


:::
:::


Monthly instalments due on the last day of the month show why this matters.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
jan <- ymd_hms("2025-01-31 03:04:05")
jan + months(1:3) # 31 February and 31 April do not exist, so NA
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] NA                        "2025-03-31 03:04:05 UTC"
[3] NA                       
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
jan %m+% months(1:3) # stops at the last day of the month
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-02-28 03:04:05 UTC" "2025-03-31 03:04:05 UTC"
[3] "2025-04-30 03:04:05 UTC"
```


:::
:::


::: callout-warning
## Caution

Adding `months()` to a date near the end of a month gives `NA` when the new date does not exist, like 31 February. In a column of due dates, such rows quietly become missing. Use `%m+%`, which stops at the last day of the month instead.
:::

### Adding with rollback

The function `add_with_rollback()` does the same, with more control. Its syntax is shown below.

```
add_with_rollback(e1, e2, roll_to_first = FALSE, preserve_hms = TRUE)
```


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- ymd_hms("2025-01-29 01:02:03")
add_with_rollback(x, months(1))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-02-28 01:02:03 UTC"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
add_with_rollback(x, months(1), preserve_hms = FALSE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-02-28 UTC"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
add_with_rollback(x, months(1), roll_to_first = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-03-01 01:02:03 UTC"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
add_with_rollback(x, months(1), roll_to_first = TRUE, preserve_hms = FALSE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-03-01 UTC"
```


:::
:::


There is no 29 February in 2025. By default, the date rolls back to the last day of February. With `roll_to_first = TRUE`, it moves to the first day of March instead. `preserve_hms` decides whether the time of day is kept.

### Coercing one time span unit to another

Time spans in `lubridate` can be converted from one class to another with these functions.

- `as.period(x, unit)`
- `as.duration(x)`
- `as.interval(x, start)`
- `make_difftime(x)`


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# A period follows the calendar
(per <- days(31))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "31d 0H 0M 0S"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
(int1 <- as.interval(per, dmy("01022024")))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2024-02-01 UTC--2024-03-03 UTC
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# A duration is an exact length of time
(dur <- ddays(31))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2678400s (~4.43 weeks)"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
(int2 <- as.interval(dur, dmy("01022024")))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2024-02-01 UTC--2024-03-03 UTC
```


:::
:::


## Rounding date-time variables

Three functions round dates and date-times to a unit of time.

- `floor_date()` rounds down to the start of the unit.
- `ceiling_date()` rounds up to the start of the next unit.
- `round_date()` rounds to the nearest boundary of the unit.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- ymd_hms("2024-08-03 12:01:59.23")
round_date(x, "month")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-08-01 UTC"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
round_date(x, "week")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-08-04 UTC"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
floor_date(x, "day")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-08-03 UTC"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ceiling_date(x, "month")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2024-09-01 UTC"
```


:::
:::


`floor_date(x, "month")` is especially useful. It turns every date into the first day of its month, which makes monthly totals easy, as we see in the chart below.

Three more functions roll a date forward or backward to a month end.

- `rollbackward()` moves a date to the last day of the previous month, or to the first day of its own month.
- `rollforward()` moves a date to the last day of its month, or to the first day of the next month. Optionally, the time of day can be kept.
- `rollback()` is another name for `rollbackward()`.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
date <- ymd_hms("2025-03-03 12:44:22")

rollbackward(date)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-02-28 12:44:22 UTC"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
rollbackward(date, roll_to_first = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-03-01 12:44:22 UTC"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
rollbackward(date, preserve_hms = FALSE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-02-28 UTC"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
rollbackward(date, roll_to_first = TRUE, preserve_hms = FALSE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-03-01 UTC"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
rollforward(date)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-03-31 12:44:22 UTC"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
rollforward(date, roll_to_first = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-04-01 12:44:22 UTC"
```


:::
:::


`rollforward()` gives the last day of the month. This is how the date of retirement is worked out in @sec-validate, since a government servant retires on the last day of the month in which he or she attains 60.

## Representing date and date-times in customised formats

Once R recognises a date, it always prints it in the same way, however it was written in the source.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
(date1 <- dmy("01-01-2025"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-01-01"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
(date2 <- ymd("2025/01/01"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-01-01"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
as.character(date1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2025-01-01"
```


:::
:::


In the console, all dates print in the `yyyy-mm-dd` form. Reports, however, often need another format, like `15 August 2024` or `15/08/2024`. The functions `format()` and `strftime()` turn dates and date-times into text in any format we give. The codes are those in @tbl-lubri001 in @sec-strpp.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
format(as.Date("2024-08-15"), "%d %B %Y")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "15 August 2024"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
format(as.Date("2024-08-15"), "%d/%m/%Y")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "15/08/2024"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
strftime(as.Date("2024-08-15"), "%A, %d %B %Y")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Thursday, 15 August 2024"
```


:::
:::


`lubridate` has a friendlier way too. The functions `stamp()`, `stamp_date()` and `stamp_time()` take an example sentence and make a *function* which formats dates in the same way.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
paid_dates  <- dmy(c("15-08-2024", "26-01-2025", "02-10-2024"))
paid_stamp  <- stamp_date("Paid on 5 March 2024")
paid_stamp(paid_dates)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Paid on 15 August 2024"  "Paid on 26 January 2025"
[3] "Paid on 02 October 2024"
```


:::
:::


This is handy for sentences in audit observations and letters.

## Dates in ggplot2 visualisations

Dates and date-times are continuous values with labels in a particular format. So ggplot2 has two special scale functions for them.

- `scale_x_date()`
- `scale_x_datetime()`

The arguments `date_breaks` and `date_minor_breaks` place the breaks by units of time. For example, `date_breaks = "3 months"` puts a major tick mark every three months. The argument `date_labels` sets the format of the labels, using the codes of @tbl-lubri001. Charts are explained in detail in @sec-ggplot2.

Let us chart the amount paid each month from the bill register. `floor_date()` turns each payment date into its month.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
bill_register |>
  filter(!is.na(paid)) |>
  mutate(month = floor_date(paid, "month")) |>
  summarise(amount_lakh = sum(amount) / 1e5, .by = month) |>
  ggplot(aes(month, amount_lakh)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %Y",
               date_breaks = "3 months",
               date_minor_breaks = "1 month") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Amount paid (₹ lakh)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Audit use case, date-based tests {#sec-lubri-audit}

Let us now apply these functions to three tests which auditors use all the time. We use the bill register created at the start of the chapter (@sec-lubri-data).

### Financial year and its quarters

The Indian financial year runs from April to March. `lubridate`'s `quarter()` has an argument `fiscal_start`, the month in which the year starts. With `fiscal_start = 4`, April to June is the first quarter. The financial year can be labelled like `2024-25` with a little arithmetic, in a small function of our own.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
fin_year <- function(date) {
  start <- if_else(month(date) >= 4, year(date), year(date) - 1)
  paste0(start, "-", sprintf("%02d", (start + 1) %% 100))
}

tibble(date = as.Date(c("2024-03-31", "2024-04-01", "2025-01-15"))) |>
  mutate(financial_year = fin_year(date),
         fy_quarter     = quarter(date, fiscal_start = 4))
```

### Payments on Sundays and holidays

Government offices are closed on Sundays and gazetted holidays. A payment dated on such a day is unusual. It may be a back-dated entry, or a payment made without the usual checks. `wday()` gives the day of the week, and a list of holidays can be checked with `%in%`.

```{.r .cell-code}
  filter(day == "Sunday" | paid %in% holidays) |>
```

### Ageing analysis

*Ageing* sorts pending items by how long they have been pending. It is one of the most common audit analyses. It applies to pending bills, outstanding advances, unadjusted suspense entries and grievances not disposed of. Let us age the unpaid bills as on 31 March 2025.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
as_on <- as.Date("2025-03-31")

ageing <- bill_register |>
  filter(is.na(paid)) |>
  mutate(days_pending = as.numeric(as_on - received),
         age_group = cut(days_pending,
                         breaks = c(-Inf, 30, 90, 180, 365, Inf),
                         labels = c("Up to 30 days", "31-90 days", "91-180 days",
                                    "181-365 days", "Over a year")))

age_summary <- ageing |>
  summarise(bills = n(), amount_lakh = round(sum(amount) / 1e5, 2), .by = age_group) |>
  arrange(age_group)
age_summary
```

Always fix the *as-on date* of an ageing analysis, as we did with `as_on`, instead of using `today()`. The analysis is then reproducible, and matches the date of the accounts being audited. ## Audit use case, approvals outside office hours {#sec-lubri-hours}

Dates tell us *which day* something happened. Date-times also tell us *what time*, and that can be just as revealing. Most computerised systems record a time stamp for every transaction. Examples are the treasury's e-payment system, an ERP and core banking. The stamp shows when a bill was passed, a payment approved or a record changed. Government offices work roughly from 9:30 in the morning to 6 in the evening on working days. A payment approved at two in the morning, or on a Sunday, is not necessarily wrong. But it deserves a question. Was the approver really at work then? Was someone else using the approver's login?

Let us take the system log of e-payment approvals of a treasury for one quarter.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Code to create the approval log"}
set.seed(915)
work_days <- seq(as.Date("2024-10-01"), as.Date("2024-12-31"), by = "day")
work_days <- work_days[!wday(work_days) %in% c(1, 7)]       # Monday to Friday
users <- sprintf("USR%02d", 1:12)
n_log <- 6000
approval_log <- tibble(
  user = sample(users, n_log, TRUE),
  # mostly between 10 am and 6 pm, peaking before lunch and in the late afternoon
  time = force_tz(as_datetime(sample(work_days, n_log, TRUE)), "Asia/Kolkata") +
         round(3600 * pmin(pmax(rnorm(n_log, 14, 2.1), 9.6), 19.5) * 60) / 60,
  amount = round(rlnorm(n_log, log(40000), 1))
)
# Planted. One user approves payments late at night and at weekends
odd_days <- seq(as.Date("2024-10-01"), as.Date("2024-12-31"), by = "day")
odd <- tibble(
  user = "USR07",
  time = force_tz(as_datetime(sample(odd_days, 45, TRUE)), "Asia/Kolkata") +
         3600 * sample(c(22, 23, 0, 1, 2), 45, TRUE) + 60 * sample(0:59, 45, TRUE),
  amount = round(rlnorm(45, log(180000), 0.6))
)
approval_log <- bind_rows(approval_log, odd) |> arrange(time)
```

## Audit tip

Before reading anything into the hours, check the **time zone** of the time stamps. Systems often store time in UTC, which is five and a half hours behind Indian Standard Time. Read in the wrong zone, a 3 pm approval appears as 9:30 am, and every pattern shifts. Use `with_tz(time, "Asia/Kolkata")` to show a stored time in Indian time. Use `force_tz()` when a time was recorded without a zone and is known to be Indian time. The trap is easy to fall into. Even `as.POSIXct()` on a date gives midnight in UTC, which is 5:30 am in India. While preparing the data for this very section, that one slip moved every approval five and a half hours later. It made the whole office look as if it worked through the night. The code above uses `force_tz(as_datetime(date), "Asia/Kolkata")`, which gives midnight in Indian time.
:::

## A suggested workflow

1.  **Read the dates correctly.** Dates in files received from the auditee come in many forms. Use `dmy()`, `ymd()` or `mdy()` to match the order in the file, and check a few rows after conversion. Turn Excel serial numbers into dates with `as.Date(x, origin = "1899-12-30")`.
2.  **Look for impossible dates.** Dates that fail to parse, like 30 February, become `NA`. Count them, and treat them as findings.
3.  **Set the time zone.** Time stamps from a system log may be stored in UTC. Use `with_tz()` or `force_tz()` to get Indian Standard Time before any analysis.
4.  **Add the financial year and quarter.** Use `quarter()` with `fiscal_start = 4`, so that April to June is the first quarter. Then summarise bills and payments by financial year and quarter.
5.  **Check payments on Sundays and holidays.** Use `wday()` to find the day of the week, and `%in%` to compare with the list of gazetted holidays. Check both, since a holiday can fall on a weekday.
6.  **Look at the hour of approvals.** Use `hour()` on the time stamps to find approvals made late at night or at weekends. Count them by user.
7.  **Check dates against periods.** Use `%within%` to check that supplies fall within the contract period, and `int_overlaps()` to find contracts that clash.
8.  **Run validity checks.** Subtract dates to get the days taken to pay. A bill paid before it was received is either an entry error or an advance payment, and needs explanation.
9.  **Age the pending items.** Fix an as-on date, work out the days pending, and sort them into age groups with `cut()`. Make the groups match the time limits in the rules.

::: callout-important
## Remember

Dates and times are easy to misread. A wrong date order or a wrong time zone shifts every result, without any error message. Check a few converted values by hand. Use periods and `%m+%` for calendar arithmetic, so that due dates do not go missing. Fix the as-on date instead of using `today()`, so that the analysis can be repeated.
:::
